name: Algerian
description: Algerian (or Algerian Patience) is a grand, two-deck solitaire game noted for its complex layout and unique 'dual-direction' foundations. Unlike most solitaires that build in one direction, Algerian requires players to manage four foundations ascending from Ace and four descending from King simultaneously. With a wrapping tableau and a multi-stage redeal mechanic, it is a game of deep tactical planning and endurance.

history.origins: First documented by the author 'Tarbart' in the 1905 publication 'Games of Patience'. Its name suggests an exotic origin, though it is more likely an English invention from the Victorian/Edwardian era fascination with North African themes.
timeline: 1905: Tarbart publishes the first known ruleset.
1979: David Parlett includes it in the 'Penguin Book of Patience', standardizing the modern rules.
2000s: Becomes a popular advanced level in computer solitaire collections like PySol.
history.cultural: Regarded by solitaire enthusiasts as a 'mental exercise' game rather than a quick pastime, often played in serious competition formats.
history.evolution: The game evolved as a more complex alternative to 'Tournament', adding more cells and the distinctive wrap-around building logic.

setup.players: One player only. Algerian is a solitaire (patience) game played by a single player.
setup.deck: Two standard 52-card decks shuffled together (104 cards).
setup.dealing: 1. **Foundations**: 8 slots (initially empty or 4 Aces/4 Kings placed if drawn). 2. **Tableau**: 8 depots with 1 card each. 3. **Reserve**: 6 piles with 4 cards each. 4. **Stock**: Remainder of the 104 cards.

rules.objective: Consolidate all 104 cards into the 8 foundation piles (A-K and K-A).
rules.gameplay: 1. Deal layout: 8 tableau depots (1 card each), 6 reserve piles (4 cards each), stock = remainder. 2. Play phase: Move exposed top cards from reserve or tableau to foundations (4 A-up, 4 K-down in suit) or build on tableau in ascending/descending suit (wrap King-Ace). Vacant depots accept any exposed card. Reserve piles cannot be built on. 3. Redeal: When no moves, deal 2 more cards to each reserve; repeat until 8 cards left, then 1 per depot. 4. Win when all 104 cards are on foundations.
keyRules: The reserve piles cannot be built upon; they only serve as sources of cards.
Empty tableau depots can be filled by ANY available card.
The game is won only when ALL cards are on foundations.

strategy.basic: Prioritize emptying the reserve piles. Since you cannot build on them, they act as bottlenecks that hide 24 cards at the start.
strategy.intermediate: Manage your foundations evenly. If you build one suit too far up, you might find that the corresponding descending foundation for that suit is blocked by cards you've already 'packed away'.
strategy.advanced: Utilization of the 'Meeting Point': Strategic transfers between the ascending and descending foundations can be used to free up a specific card needed for the tableau.
tips: Avoid filling empty tableau spaces immediately. Keep them as 'temporary parking' for cards that are blocking deep reserve piles.
Because you can build both up and down, try to keep 'middle' cards (7, 8, 9) on the tableau where they have the most building options.

variations.name: Carthage
variations.description: Similar to Algerian but with slightly different stock-dealing rules and no wrapping on the tableau.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Carthage is noted as a related variant but its detailed engine overrides are not yet modeled.

scoring.description: Scoring is based on the total cards moved to foundations.

sources.name: David Parlett - Penguin Book of Patience

synthesis.shortDescription: Tackle one of the most intellectually demanding solitaires ever devised. Algerian Patience tasks you with building UP and DOWN across eight foundations. With a unique wrapping tableau and stock deals that can change everything, only a true master of planning will clear the 104-card layout.
